newsitem.title: USA: Ill. agency okays details for Allstate bond deals.
newsitem.headline: Ill. agency okays details for Allstate bond deals.

text.p: The Illinois Development Finance Authority board on Wednesday gave a thumbs up to new parameters for a non-profit bond program involving Allstate Insurance Co, a unit of Allstate Corp.
While the board did not take a formal vote on the parameters, a poll of members by board chairman Harry Seigle revealed no problems with the plan.

Under the innovative program, Allstate would participate in a public/private relationship allowing it to purchase bonds of social service agencies in Illinois with limited credit enhancement provided by the authority.

Some board members had expressed concern about how the credit enhancement would work at the agency's December board meeting in view of different parameters suggested by Allstate, Gov Jim Edgar's office and the authority.

Bobby Wilkerson, the agency's director, said the new parameters addressed those concerns by applying the agency's credit enhancement funds to pooled deals on an aggregate basis and on non-pooled deals on a per deal basis.
He added that the amount of reserve the authority would provide for each deal would range from seven to 10 percent depending on the deal.
In addition, the reserve would stay in place for 10 years even if the authority's participation in the deal is bought out by a social service agency, according to Wilkerson.

Wilkerson said the new parameters would now go through the approval process at Allstate. He added that the first bond deal under the program could come to the board for approval as early as next month. That deal would involve $15 million of tax-exempt bonds for a group of agencies on Chicago's southside called CARES.
An Allstate executive has said the authority's role in structuring the deals and providing credit enhancement were key to the company's interest in the program.

The aim of the program is to give social service providers that are largely dependent on state contracts access to the debt market at lower costs by eliminating the need for a letter of credit or bond insurance.
